The audit

{{n_checks_cap}} checks, {{n_datasets}} published benchmarks, and {{n_pass_with_train_word}} that nothing was flagged on.

We pointed the tool at the benchmarks people already train on. {{n_collections_cap}} collections, curated into one format and put through the same {{n_checks_word}} checks — so these are measurements on published data, browsable per dataset, with the report behind every number.

  • {{n_datasets}} Datasets audited, across {{n_collections_word}} collections Curated from {{n_curated}}; {{n_excluded}} could not be put through the same {{n_checks_word}} checks
  • {{n_fail}} Flagged Fail on at least one of the {{n_checks_word}} checks {{n_warning}} rolled up to Warning, {{n_pass}} to Pass
  • {{median_probe_auroc}} Median AUROC recovered by one hand-crafted feature on its own {{n_probe_over_0_7}} of the {{n_probed}} probed datasets reach 0.70 or more from one feature
  • {{n_leakage_over_50}} Datasets where half or more of the held-out split is also in training {{n_with_any_leakage}} of the {{n_leakage_scanned}} scanned have at least one sequence in two splits

{{n_pass_with_train_cap}} of the {{n_with_train}} datasets that define a training split had nothing flagged on any check. That is not a statement about the rest, and a Pass is not a guarantee about a dataset: it establishes that these {{n_checks_word}} checks do not separate the classes, so every number above is a lower bound on what a learned model could recover. A check reports what it measured and not what caused it, and a compositional difference between classes may be genuine biology.

The aggregate is not the useful part. What tells you what to control for is the name of the feature that separated your benchmark and the distribution it was measured on — so the audit is published per dataset, not as a headline. That is what the rest of this page is.

How results are flagged

{{n_probe_checks_cap}} of the {{n_checks_word}} checks ask one narrow question: could a classifier that saw only this one feature tell the two classes apart? Nothing is trained. The feature is the score, so its AUROC answers directly — 0.5 is a feature that says nothing about the classes, 1.0 is one that settles them on its own — and a flag is a boundary drawn on that number.

The boundaries genomic-benchmarks-qc puts on a probe AUROC. Every probe mark in the grid above was decided by them.
Flag AUROC Read it as
Pass ≤ 0.60 The classes are not separable along this feature
Warning 0.60 – 0.70 A model could get some traction here
Fail > 0.70 Separable from this one feature alone
Unknown — The comparison was not made, which is not a Pass

Two guards sit in front of the scoring, and a check that trips one returns Unknown rather than a number: nothing is scored on fewer than 250 sequences per class, and a per-position comparison stops where fewer than a quarter of the class is long enough to reach that position — past there the sequences being compared are a sample of the long ones rather than of the class. What a check reports is the worst of its sub-checks and not their average, so a Fail on per-position nucleotide content can be one base at one position out of hundreds, which is what the report behind it is for.

Neither the {{n_integrity_checks_word}} integrity checks nor the leakage scan is scored that way. Unique bases asks whether both classes use the same alphabet; the two duplicate checks are thresholds on how much of a class survives deduplication, and on whether any sequence appears under both labels; and the leakage scan counts the sequences of one split that are also present in another.

That is the short version. How a flag is decided gives the rules in full, including the simulations the 0.60 boundary comes from; what this run measured, and on which split, is on the methods page.
